title: Getting in front of the police masking controversy
summary: Authorities need to think twice about the optics of heavily armed immigration officers with face coverings conducting raids in our communities, writes Karl Bickel, or risk undermining public trust, even among those who normally support the police.
content:
by Karl Bickel, Maryland Matters August 6, 2025

by Karl Bickel, Maryland Matters August 6, 2025

In the wake of the unprecedented, often indiscriminate roundup of undocumented immigrants by the Department of Homeland Security’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE),  the masking of law enforcement officers has become a hot-button issue. While casting their wide net, heavily armed masked ICE agents have instilled an unparalleled fear in many communities throughout the country.

The wearing of masks by ICE agents has had a chilling effect on communities where agents have conducted raids, particularly when naturalized and native-born citizens have been caught up in their net. The intentional fear that is generated by ICE agents is damaging to local law enforcement. It erodes the police/community trust necessary for state and local law enforcement to effectively do its job.

The optics of heavily armed law enforcement officers with face coverings conducting raids in our communities undermines public trust, even among those who are typically supportive of the police. It is antithetical to community policing which requires trust in order to build collaborative partnerships that address crime and public order problems.

In law enforcement bad actions and bad policies tend to metastasize and infect other agencies. This has been exemplified by excessive uses of force, dangerous vehicle pursuit policies and various aspects of the over-militarization that has taken place in many police departments. Among the bad habits that some agencies may be facing in these uncertain times is the masking of law enforcement personnel as they carry out their duties.

Using a mask to conceal the identity of officers may unintentionally reinforce existing negative perceptions of the police at a time when confidence in America’s institutions is in decline. According to Gallup organization polling, the average confidence in American institutions remains low at 28% while confidence in police has reached 51%. If the masking of local police is not curbed this level of confidence in police is unlikely to be sustained, a level of confidence that is necessary to keep our communities safe through a cooperative trusting relationship between police and those they serve.

Two states that have taken measures to prevent the damage caused by masking of law enforcement are California, with its No Secret Police Act, Senate Bill SB 627, and Massachusetts House Docket (HD) 4886, both of which prohibit the wearing of masks by police except in certain circumstances.

In both of the aforementioned bills it would be a “crime for a law enforcement officer to wear any mask or personal disguise while interacting with the public in the performance of their duties, except as specified.” The bills define law enforcement officers as any officer of a local, state, federal law enforcement agency, or any person acting on behalf of a local, state, or federal law enforcement agency.

Exemptions from these provisions include an officer engaged in an undercover assignment, medical masks as well as ones designed to protect against smoke or toxins and those worn by SWAT members to protect themselves.

As the summer turns to fall and our state legislators flesh out an agenda for the 2026 legislative session, placing limits on Maryland’s law enforcement officers’ use of masks, balaclavas and neck gaiters should be on their radar screen.
